DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on
Designing Decomposition Algorithms
Sikai Cheng∗†, Tinghan Ye∗, Arnaud Deza, Xiaonan Qi, Miao Li, Litong Liu, Changkun Guan
Georgia Institute of Technology
∗Equal contribution
†Corresponding author
§ github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym
# sikaicheng@gatech.edu
October 30, 2026
Abstract
Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and
dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language
models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for
new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement
these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five
Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet
three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which
an LLM judge reads the solver’s code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12
GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent
regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance
and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most
common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108
attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimality claim made without proof, occurs 96
times, 92 of them in one model. Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration,
and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defect, far more often than objective gaps.
Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the
error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.

DecompGym
1 Introduction
Many large optimization problems in operations research are solved by decomposition. Benders decomposition
fixes complicating decisions in a master problem and adds cuts generated by subproblems [5, 54]. Column
generation solves a restricted master problem over a subset of columns and adds columns found by a pricing
subproblem that uses the master’s dual values [16, 43]. Both algorithms are difficult to implement. The master
and subproblems must be formulated consistently; duals, cuts, or columns must pass correctly between them;
and the stopping rule must match what the final solution certifies. An error in any of these steps can leave a
program that runs and returns a plausible answer.
Large language models are now used to automate parts of algorithm design. Program-search methods
evolve heuristics and algorithms with an LLM in the loop [41, 50, 56, 72]. In operations research, LLMs
formulate optimization models [13, 71], design algorithms that match or beat published methods on most
instances of inventory, queueing, and assortment problems [3], search over inventory policy classes [70], and
act as preference oracles inside multi-objective selection algorithms [35]. Recent benchmarks evaluate coding
agents on writing complete solvers for operations research tasks [36, 39]. These advances point toward agents
that design and implement decomposition algorithms for new problems.
Building such agents first requires knowing how well current coding agents design and implement these
algorithms and how they fail. This paper is an exploratory study of both. Existing evaluations let the agent
choose the method and score the solution or policy it returns. Studies of coding agents show that passing tests
does not imply meeting the specification when shortcuts are available [22, 74, 76]. For decomposition, output
checks credit two kinds of solver that violate the method contract: one that reaches the optimal objective
through a heuristic that bypasses the decomposition, and one that labels its solution optimal although its
algorithm has not proved it. Measuring method use therefore requires an audit of the solver’s code. We define
the method-conformance gap as the attempts that pass every output check (execution, feasibility, and objective
within 1% of the optimal objective) and fail the method audit. We measure it on ordinary tasks that plant no
shortcut.
We conduct the study on DecompGym, a set of 81 instances from nine problem families (Figure 1) drawn
from facility location, transportation, routing, stochastic planning, packing, assignment, and scheduling.
Five families are posed for Benders decomposition and four for column generation, each at three sizes with
three seeds. An agent receives an application description, instance data, an output format, and a method
contract that specifies the required master–subproblem information flow, then writes a standalone Python
solver. Each attempt is checked against three criteria in sequence: execution within a common 60-second
time limit; numerical feasibility checks together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the
solver’s code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. A paired protocol shares the first
attempt between two retry policies, independent regeneration and reflection (a separate model query that
diagnoses the failed attempt and writes advice for the next one), so both start from the same outcome.
The protocol records the attempts, time, and tokens each policy uses. DecompGym, including its instance
generators, formulations, reference implementations, reference solutions, and the evaluation code, is available
at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.
1.1 Main findings
We evaluate 12 models: five GPT, six Claude, and one Gemini. Each runs inside its provider’s coding-agent
tool, so its results reflect both the model and the tool. The main findings are as follows.
• Two models implement verified decompositions on every first attempt. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol
pass every instance on their first attempt, and seven models exceed 90%. First-attempt success ranges from
56.8% to 100%. With ten attempts, nine of the twelve models reach full coverage without reflection and
ten with it.
• Execution overstates capability, and the failure modes depend on the method. Of the first attempts,
99.0% run and 87.8% meet all three criteria. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal
solutions, concentrated in fixed-charge transportation. The most common column-generation failure is a
method-audit rejection, in 26 of the 57 failed column-generation first attempts.
• The method-conformance gap is 93 of the 108 attempts rejected by the method audit. These attempts
returned feasible solutions within 1% of the optimal objective, so an evaluation that checks only outputs
2


--- Page 3 ---
DecompGym
would credit them. Of the 108, 96 reported an optimal solution without proof, and Claude Sonnet 5
produced 92 of them. In 95 of the 96, a column-generation solver had optimized only over the columns
it generated and then claimed that no better solution exists. Counting these rejections as passes would
raise Claude Sonnet 5’s first-attempt successes from 46 to 66 of 81, and no other model’s by more than one
instance.
• Reflection succeeds most on failures that its feedback names. Reflection turns 66% of retries into
successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and the method audit rejects 5 of its retries, compared
with 64 under regeneration. Its remaining failures are mostly objective gaps, for which the feedback only
reports that the target is unmet.
• Time and tokens measure different costs. Among models that solve every instance without reflection,
mean agent time to success ranges from 21.5 to 228.2 seconds. Token use ranks models differently. GPT-6
Luna and GPT-5.6 Luna finish faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol but consume 2.2 to 3.2 times as
many tokens.
1.2 Implications for decomposition agents
An agent built for decomposition needs a check on how its solver reaches an answer, because an agent that tests
only its output would accept every attempt in the method-conformance gap. It also needs feedback that locates
the error. The judge’s rationale locates method-audit failures, and after such a rejection the next reflection
attempt met all three criteria in 41 of 44 cases. After an objective gap, the feedback gives no such location.
Information from the optimization itself, such as the solver’s bounds or its gap at termination, could tell the
agent where the error lies. Section 6 states the limits of the study.
2 Related Work
Optimization modeling benchmarks.
Most benchmarks for LLMs in optimization test modeling. The model
turns a natural-language problem into a formulation, a general-purpose solver solves it, and the benchmark
compares the objective or status with a reference. The datasets range from linear-programming word problems
to industrial, nonlinear, and MIPLIB-derived instances [13, 28, 30, 40, 42, 55, 71], and a survey reports high
error rates in their reference answers [68]. Systems built for these benchmarks produce the model and its code
with agent teams, fine-tuning, or solver-verified rewards [2, 12, 33, 67]. Beyond building new models, LLMs
also turn natural-language change requests into updates of a deployed model and choose how to re-optimize
it [73]. Because a general-purpose solver supplies the algorithm, these tasks never ask the model to implement
one, and the output alone decides success.
Agents that write optimization algorithms and solver code.
When agents write the solution method itself,
benchmarks score complete programs by feasibility, objective, and running time on large operations research
tasks [36, 39] or by agreement between the stated formulation and the code [21]. Others have agents write
solver components such as constraint handlers, cut selectors, and branching rules [49, 69], or heuristics scored
by solution quality [10, 32, 61], and algorithm-design studies search over programs or policy classes with
an evaluator [3, 41, 50, 56, 70, 72]. In all of this work the agent chooses the method and the output or its
performance decides success. FrontierOR observes that stronger models more often choose decomposition or
hybrid methods, and ORAgentBench notes that it lacks a process-level audit [36, 39]. Benchmarks that do
prescribe a method come from machine-learning research code, where PaperBench and ResearchCodeBench
grade implementations of a described method with rubrics and unit tests [27, 60]. DecompGym brings this
kind of evaluation to optimization algorithms by prescribing the decomposition and checking the solver’s code
against it.
Decomposition methods and their automation.
Decades of work have refined both methods. Benders
variants strengthen the cuts or extend the method to nonlinear, logic-based, and big-M subproblems [14, 24,
26, 45], as surveyed by Rahmaniani et al. [54]. Column-generation research covers bounds, stabilization,
branching, and integer solutions [43], and branch-and-price embeds column generation in branch-and-
bound [4]. Solvers and learned models automate parts of applying a decomposition. GCG, SCIP, and CPLEX
3


--- Page 4 ---
DecompGym
run a Dantzig–Wolfe or Benders decomposition when the user supplies the structure or the solver detects
it [7, 8, 23, 46], and learned models decide whether to decompose or which columns to add [6, 37, 48]. These
tools need a model whose block structure is given or detectable, and they run a fixed implementation. An
agent in DecompGym receives a problem description and must write the master, the subproblems, and their
coordination.
Specification conformance, false success, and judge validity.
Coding-agent benchmarks score software
changes with tests [34], and several studies show that agents can pass tests without meeting the specification.
The evidence comes from tasks in which the tests conflict with the specification or held-out tests differ from
visible ones [74, 76], from measured rates of hardcoding, test editing, and reward hacking [22, 31, 62, 65],
and from agents’ status reports, which are often false [1, 59]. Closest to our setting, LLM-written combinatorial
solvers replace complete search with approximations or unverified bounds [66]. Most of these studies plant a
shortcut or make one available, and they do not measure how often output checks miss method failures on
ordinary optimization tasks. Measuring this rate requires a judge. LLM judges agree with humans on most
comparisons but show position, verbosity, and self-preference biases [52, 75]; they detect false success poorly
from agent trajectories and reliably from clear code-level cheating [1, 22]. The DecompGym judge reads solver
source, which is closer to the code-level setting.
Reflection and repair.
Reflection methods give an agent verbal feedback on its earlier attempts before it
tries again [11, 44, 58]. Their benefit depends on where the feedback comes from and how cost is counted.
Models do not improve their reasoning through self-correction without external feedback [29], self-repair
gains in code generation are modest once the repair step is charged [51], and repeated sampling with a verifier
raises coverage log-linearly in the number of samples [9]. In DecompGym, regeneration is repeated sampling
with the benchmark’s evaluation as verifier, and reflection receives external feedback from execution and the
method audit. Both policies start from the same first attempt, and the benchmark records the attempts, time,
and tokens each uses.
3 The DecompGym Benchmark
Each DecompGym task gives a coding agent one instance of an optimization problem and a prescribed
decomposition method, and asks for a solver that applies that method.
A task consists of an application description, the instance data in a structured file, a prescribed method
family, and an output contract. The agent writes a Python solver that reads the instance and outputs an
objective value and the decisions needed for verification. The permitted libraries are Gurobi’s Python interface,
NumPy, and the Python standard library. The agent designs the decomposition from this specification and
writes all of the solver’s code.
Table 1 lists the nine families. Five are posed for Benders decomposition and four for column genera-
tion, so each method is exercised on several distinct master–subproblem structures. Among the Benders
families, uncapacitated facility location (UFL) has a well-studied Benders decomposition [20], fixed-charge
transportation (FCTP) is a fixed-charge network design problem, a class to which Benders decomposition is
widely applied [15], 𝑘-median (KM) admits an efficient Benders decomposition [18], and stochastic planning
(TSSO) follows the two-stage L-shaped structure [38, 63]. Location routing (LRP) combines depot location
with route selection [53]; its route-selection subproblem is integer, so linear-programming cuts give only a
bound, and closing the gap calls for logic-based Benders cuts [19, 26]. Among the column-generation families,
cutting stock (CSP) is the original column-generation problem [25], generalized assignment (GAP) has a
branch-and-price literature [57], shift scheduling (SHIFT) is solved by branch-and-price over a set-covering
formulation [47], and bin packing (BP) and cutting stock are studied with branch-and-price and other exact
methods [17, 64]. Appendix A gives each family’s model and the formulation of its reference decomposition.
Each family is instantiated at three size levels with three seeds, for 45 Benders and 36 column-generation
instances in total. Size levels are defined by the generator settings within each family. The instances are of
moderate dimension, and every solver an agent writes must finish within 60 seconds; a hand-written reference
implementation of each prescribed decomposition meets all three criteria within this limit (Appendix A).
The benchmark measures whether an agent implements the prescribed method correctly, and the time limit
4


--- Page 5 ---
DecompGym
also requires that implementation to be reasonably efficient. Every model receives the same inputs, prompts,
and output schemas and is scored against the same stored optimal objectives. Appendix B lists the realized
dimensions.
A Benders implementation must fix master decisions in the subproblems and feed subproblem information
back to the master through feasibility or optimality cuts. Classical, integer, and logic-based variants are
permitted [26, 38]. A column-generation implementation must pass restricted-master dual information to
pricing and use the resulting columns in subsequent master solves. Legitimate initialization, immediate
convergence, and final integer restricted-master solves are allowed. A separate monolithic solve of the full
original problem is prohibited anywhere in the solver, including the initial solution and any backup procedure.
The contract also requires mutually consistent decisions and objective values, and a reported status that
matches what the algorithm proves: the label optimal requires a proof that no better solution exists, and any
other solution must be labeled feasible. The method contract states this rule in its closing sentence (Prompt 1).
4 Evaluation Protocol
Each of the twelve models attempts all 81 instances under two retry policies, and three criteria score every
attempt in order.
The study evaluates five GPT models through OpenAI’s Codex command-line tool, six Claude models
through Claude Code, and Gemini 3.8 Flash through Google’s Antigravity command-line tool, all at medium
reasoning effort; Table 2 lists the twelve. Every agent call runs in a new Docker container with a fresh
workspace, and no conversation history, memory, user configuration, or extensions carry over from earlier calls.
Each solver the agent writes runs with one solver thread and a 60-second limit that covers setup, all master
and subproblem solves, and writing the output. The method judge is a separate GPT-6 Astra query at high
reasoning effort. Appendix I lists software versions and limits.
The first attempt on each instance is shared by the two policies (Figure 1). In the regeneration policy,
each later attempt starts a new session from the original task and data, so each retry is independent of earlier
attempts. In the reflection policy, a separate diagnosis call to the same model first reads the failed code, its
execution output, and the judge’s rationale and writes advice. The next attempt receives the previous code
together with that advice. When the objective misses the target, the diagnosis prompt states only that the
objective must improve. Each policy stops at the first success or after ten attempts.
Execution (E) requires the solver to run without error within the time limit and write its output file.
Verification (V) adds two checks. The output must report a finite objective and pass problem-specific numerical
checks of feasibility, integrality, consistency, and the recomputed objective, and the method judge must accept
the code. The judge reads the solver’s source and the method contract given to the agent, checks whether
Table 1. Nine task families, with nine instances per family. BD denotes Benders decomposition; CG denotes column
generation. The decomposition-structure column summarizes what the master decides and what the subproblems return
to it; Appendix A states the formulations.
Method

--- Page 6 ---
DecompGym
the code implements the prescribed decomposition and whether its iterative master–subproblem procedure
actually produces the reported solution, and returns a verdict with a written rationale. Quality (Q) adds
that the recomputed objective lies within 1% of the stored optimal objective, which the agent never sees. An
attempt succeeds when it meets all three criteria.
Results are reported by attempt budget. An instance counts as solved at budget 𝑘(written Q@𝑘for the
quality criterion) when one of its first 𝑘attempts succeeds, and every rate keeps all 81 instances in the
denominator at every budget. Pooled counts cover the 972 model–instance pairs. Appendix C gives the formal
definitions and the counting conventions.
Cost is measured by agent time and tokens. Agent time is the time the agent spends writing solvers and
diagnosing failures, up to success or the last allowed attempt; judge time and solver run time are reported
separately. Token counts follow each tool’s own accounting. Appendix H breaks the recorded time down by
stage and defines the token fields of each tool.
To locate failures, each attempt is assigned to the first check it fails: execution, a numerical check, the
method audit, or the objective target. Each method rejection is classified by hand, from the judge’s rationale,
into one of three findings: an unproven optimality claim, an inactive decomposition, or a solution bypass
(Appendix E).

5.1 Can agents design and implement decomposition algorithms?
Seven of the twelve models exceed 90% first-attempt quality success, and GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol meet
all three criteria on every instance at their first attempt (Table 2). Across all models, 853 of 972 first attempts
(87.8%) succeed. First-attempt success is lowest for Claude Sonnet 5 (56.8%) and GPT-5.6 Luna (67.9%).
Retries recover 110 of the 119 failed pairs under regeneration and 117 under reflection. With up to ten
attempts, nine models solve every instance without reflection and ten with reflection, and pooled success rises
to 99.1% and 99.8%, respectively. Figure 2 shows that models with the same final coverage can need different
numbers of attempts to reach it. Because final coverage is near saturation, first-attempt success and the cost of
reaching a success separate the models.

5.2 Where do agents fail?
Of the 119 failed first attempts, 109 run to completion and fail a later criterion, so executable code is a weak
signal of a correct decomposition. Figure 3 assigns each first attempt to the first check it fails and separates the
two methods. Of the 62 Benders failures, 48 are missing or suboptimal solutions. Thirty attempts run without
returning a finite objective, typically by reporting an error or declaring a feasible instance infeasible, and 18
return feasible solutions that miss the 1% target. Fixed-charge transportation (FCTP) accounts for 19 of the 30
missing objectives and 9 of the 18 objective gaps. It is the hardest family, with 76 of its 108 first attempts
succeeding, compared with 92 to 104 for every other family. GPT-6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Luna each solve only
one of its nine instances on the first attempt. In column generation, the largest category, 26 of the 57 failed
first attempts, has a feasible output but fails the method audit; seven further method rejections also fail a
numerical check and are counted under that check. Appendix F breaks first-attempt success down by model
and family, and Appendix D reports the cumulative execution, verification, and quality curves of every model.

The method audit catches failures that output checks cannot see. Table 3 groups all 108 rejections by
finding. The most common finding, with 96 cases, is an unproven optimality claim. In the typical case, a
7


--- Page 8 ---
DecompGym
column-generation solver takes Gurobi’s optimal status for the final integer restricted master as proof of global
optimality. Section 5.3 works through an example and Appendix E.1 gives the argument. Eight rejections
identify decomposition loops that never run or cannot influence the master. Four rejections identify a heuristic
or full enumeration that produces the reported solution outside the decomposition; Appendix E gives examples
of both. Of the 108 rejected attempts, 93 returned feasible solutions within 1% of the optimal objective and
would pass an output-only evaluation; these 93 attempts form the method-conformance gap.
One model accounts for nearly all unproven optimality claims. Claude Sonnet 5 makes 92 of the 96, and
they account for 26 of its 30 first-attempt column-generation failures (Table 7). It passes 40 of 45 Benders
instances on the first attempt but only 6 of 36 column-generation instances. No other model makes the claim
more than twice across all of its attempts, so the requirement is attainable under the same prompt. Output
checks alone would credit Claude Sonnet 5 with 20 more first-attempt successes (66 instead of 46 of 81;
Section 5.6), and only an audit of the code shows which model is affected. A benchmark that prescribes a
method should verify it and report the method-conformance gap.

5.3 A case study: unproven optimality in column generation
On the medium cutting-stock instance with seed 0, Claude Sonnet 5’s first attempt returns 87 stock pieces,
which equals the optimal objective, and labels its solution optimal. It takes that label from Gurobi’s status for
the final integer restricted master, the integer program over the patterns generated so far. That status means
only that no better integer solution exists using those patterns. Because the objective is integer, the solution
is proved optimal only when 𝑧IP(𝐾), the value of the integer restricted master over the generated patterns
𝐾, equals ⌈𝑧LP⌉, where 𝑧LP is the linear relaxation value after pricing converges (Appendix E.1 derives these
bounds). The attempt passes the execution, feasibility, and objective checks. Its optimality claim may be true,
but the code never compares the two bounds. The judge rejects it with the rationale reproduced in Prompt 4.
A conforming solver labels its solution feasible unless it can close this gap, and a feasible label is never
penalized. After reading the rationale, the reflection step writes the advice in Prompt 7. The reflection
policy’s second attempt returns the same 87 pieces and labels them optimal only if pricing has converged and
𝑧IP(𝐾) = ⌈𝑧LP⌉, with 𝑧LP taken from the last linear relaxation. The judge accepts it. The two attempts return
identical outputs, and only the second attempt’s code proves the optimality it reports. Claude Sonnet 5.5
and GPT-6 Astra perform this bound check in their first attempts on this instance. Without reflection, Claude
Sonnet 5 repeats the first attempt’s status rule in all ten attempts.
5.4 When does reflection help?
Reflection mainly speeds recovery, especially from failures whose feedback names the defect. Of the 119 pairs
whose shared first attempt fails, a single reflection retry solves 94, compared with 67 for regeneration (Q@2
of 947 versus 920 of 972). By budget three, reflection solves 963 pairs, a level regeneration reaches only
at budget ten. Regeneration catches up with more attempts, so the 27-pair advantage at budgets two and
three narrows to seven at budget ten (970 versus 963). Part of this advantage depends on the status rule
(Section 5.6). Figure 4 shows the advantage at the attempt level. Reflection turns 117 of its 176 retries (66%)
into successes, compared with 110 of 281 (39%) under regeneration. The difference is largest for method
rejections. Regeneration starts each retry from the original task, and the audit rejects 64 of its retries, 63 of
them for an unproven optimality claim. Under reflection, the diagnosis step reads the judge’s rationale and
passes its advice to the retry. After a method rejection, the next reflection attempt passes the method audit
8


--- Page 9 ---
DecompGym
in 42 of 44 cases, compared with 40 of 101 under regeneration (Table 11), and the audit rejects only five
reflection retries in total. For Claude Sonnet 5, reflection raises Q@3 from 61 to 78 of 81 instances. Reflection
retries also receive the previous solver, and the protocol does not separate its effect from that of the rationale
and the advice.

Objective gaps account for 43 of the 59 unsuccessful reflection retries, concentrated in FCTP (28) and
two-stage stochastic planning (11; Table 12). For these attempts, the feedback says only that the objective
misses the target. The two pairs that remain unsolved after ten reflection attempts, GPT-6 Luna on a medium
TSSO instance and Claude Sonnet 5 on a large FCTP instance, both end with this kind of failure. The benefit
of reflection also varies across models. GPT-6 Luna, whose failures are mostly objective gaps, solves 75 of 81
instances within three attempts with reflection and 76 without it, and reaches higher coverage with reflection
only at budget ten (80 versus 77). Figure 11 (Appendix G) reports the paired gains of every model at budgets
two and three.
5.5 What does success cost?
Agent time separates models that tie on success. Table 4 reports the mean agent time and recorded tokens
per instance through success or exhaustion, and Figure 5 counts the instances whose first quality success
falls within each cumulative generation-plus-reflection time budget. Among models that solve every instance,
Claude Sonnet 5.5 needs a mean of 21.5 seconds of agent time without reflection, GPT-6 Astra 87.3 seconds,
GPT-6.1 Sol 114.8 seconds, and Gemini 3.8 Flash 228.2 seconds. Because an instance accumulates agent time
until it is solved, faster recovery also saves time: reflection lowers the mean agent time of GPT-5.6 Luna from
82.5 to 70.8 seconds and of Claude Sonnet 5 from 121.4 to 107.9 seconds, despite the extra diagnosis steps.

Recorded tokens rank the models differently from time (Figure 6). Over the eleven models with comparable
token totals, the Spearman rank correlation between mean agent time and mean tokens without reflection is
0.47. The contrast is clearest among the five GPT models, which share the Codex tool and its token accounting.
GPT-6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Luna finish in 56.7 and 82.5 seconds but consume 199.5 and 277.6 thousand tokens.
GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol take 87.3 and 114.8 seconds and consume 85.7 and 92.2 thousand. The Luna
models process 2.2 to 3.2 times as many tokens as GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Claude Sonnet 5.5 uses the
least agent time and the fewest tokens, 60.9 thousand. Reflection raises token use for nine of the eleven models
because each revision carries the previous solver and the diagnosis. Claude Sonnet 5, for example, consumes
133.3 thousand tokens with reflection and 105.1 thousand without, while its agent time falls. Token use is
unchanged for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, which never retry. Appendix H describes the time attribution and
the provider-specific token accounting.

5.6 Robustness of the findings
The unproven optimality rule determines Claude Sonnet 5’s standing. Table 9 in Appendix E.1 reports every
model’s results with these rejections counted as passes when the output was otherwise feasible and within
1% of the optimal objective. Claude Sonnet 5’s Q@1 rises from 46 to 66 of 81, and no other model’s Q@1
changes by more than one instance. Reflection’s advantage over regeneration falls from 27 to 8 pairs at budget
two (951 versus 943 of 972), from 27 to 10 at budget three (regeneration reaches 953), and from 7 to 5 at
budget ten. Claude Sonnet 5 accounts for all 17 additional regeneration successes at budget three: its count
rises from 61 to 78, equal to its reflection count.
First-attempt success varies little with instance size: 289 of the 324 pairs succeed on small instances, 283
on medium, and 281 on large (Table 10 in Appendix F).
6 Conclusion
On DecompGym, current coding agents design and implement both decomposition algorithms correctly in
853 of 972 first attempts (87.8%). GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol write Benders and column-generation solvers
that meet all three criteria on every instance at the first attempt, and seven of the twelve models succeed on
more than 90% of first attempts. The remaining failures depend on the method. Benders solvers most often
return no finite objective or a suboptimal solution, and column-generation solvers most often fail the method
audit, mainly by claiming optimality that their algorithm has not proved (92 of the 96 such claims come from
Claude Sonnet 5). Most method-audit rejections (93 of 108, the method-conformance gap) return solutions
that pass every output check, so rejecting them requires inspecting how the solver produced its answer. After a
method-audit rejection, for which the judge’s rationale names the defect, the next reflection attempt meets all
three criteria in 41 of 44 cases. It repairs only 25 of 64 objective gaps, after which the feedback says only that
the target is unmet. Time and token use separate models that reach the same final coverage.
The study uses a fixed synthetic inventory of moderate-size instances with a prescribed decomposition.
The results show which models implement the methods correctly within a common budget. How the resulting
solvers scale to larger instances is untested. Each model, instance, and policy contributes one saved trajectory,
so paired differences are descriptive and additional repetitions would estimate run-to-run variation. A single
GPT-6 Astra judge at high reasoning effort assesses method use from the source code, and GPT-6 Astra is also
11


--- Page 12 ---
DecompGym
one of the evaluated models, run in separate sessions. LLM judges can favor outputs of their own model [52].
We read every rejection rationale to categorize the findings but did not re-derive each verdict from the code.
In addition, accepted attempts were not reviewed by hand, so the rate at which the judge accepts a solver
that departs from the prescribed method is unmeasured. Agent time includes the speed of each tool and of its
provider’s service, and token totals follow provider-specific accounting.
Agents built for decomposition will need checks on how their solvers reach an answer and feedback that
locates the error, such as the bounds and gap that the solver reports at termination.

Appendix
A Problem Formulations and Reference Decompositions
This appendix states, for each family, the original optimization model and the decomposition used by the
reference implementation: the master problem, the subproblem or pricing problem, and the cut or column
returned to the master. The agents never saw these formulations. Each agent received the natural-language
task, the instance data, the output format, and the method contract in Prompt 1, and designed its own
models. The instance generators, reference implementations, stored optimal objectives, and details such as
dual signs, initialization, and convergence traces are in the DecompGym repository at https://github.com/
SIKAI-C/DecompGym.
The stored optimal objective of each instance is obtained by solving its original model, the full MIP stated
below, to optimality with Gurobi. The quality criterion compares every agent’s objective with this value.
Each reference implementation applies the prescribed decomposition under the agents’ execution conditions:
a 60-second limit on the whole solver process and one solver thread. It meets all three criteria on all 81
instances; the slowest run takes 27.25 seconds, and the largest deviation from the stored optimal objective is
0.14%. A correct decomposition therefore fits comfortably within the time limit.
The reference implementations follow the same status rule as the agents: they report “optimal” only when
their own bounds prove it. They report “optimal” on 54 instances and “feasible” on 27, and on 24 of those 27
the objective equals the stored optimal objective. A “feasible” label therefore means that the decomposition
found a solution without certifying it. The 27 include 14 column-generation instances of BP and CSP, where
16


--- Page 17 ---
DecompGym
the final integer restricted master does not reach the rounded-up linear bound; 8 TSSO instances, which stop
at a 0.5% gap between their bounds; 2 LRP instances, where the route-selection cuts give only a bound; and
one instance each of UFL, KM, and FCTP, which stop at a 0.01% target gap with the optimal objective.
Throughout, a bar denotes a value fixed by the master, a star an optimal dual solution, and a hat a dual ray.
A.1 Benders families
In each Benders family, the master chooses binary structural decisions 𝑦and an estimate 𝜃of the remaining
cost; a subproblem fixes 𝑦= ¯𝑦, solves a linear program, and returns an optimality cut or, when infeasible, a
feasibility cut. The master value is a lower bound and the best evaluated plan an upper bound; the reference
stops when they meet within tolerance.

A.2 Column-generation families
In each column-generation family, a restricted master linear program chooses weights for the columns generated
so far, and a pricing problem uses its duals to find a column with negative reduced cost. After pricing finds
none, the reference solves the master over the generated columns with integer variables. As explained in
Appendix E.1, that integer solution is proved optimal only when it attains the rounded lower bound from the
completed linear relaxation.

Each of the 972 model–instance pairs is run under both policies, giving 1,944 policy trajectories. The
shared first attempt counts toward both policies when they are compared and once in totals of agent runs, so
the failure analysis in Section 5.2 covers 1,429 physical attempts: 972 first attempts and 457 retries. Size
comparisons use 324 pairs per size level, and reflection gains are paired differences on the same instances.
Success within a time or token budget follows the same cumulative rule.

D Execution, Verification, and Quality
Table 6 reports pooled cumulative successes under each criterion, and Figure 7 shows the cumulative E, V,
and Q rates of each model. The drop from execution to quality is largest at the first attempt: 962 of 972 first
attempts run, 876 also pass verification, and 853 meet all three criteria. Retries close the execution gap first.
With reflection, every pair passes execution by budget two and verification by budget three, when nine pairs
still miss the quality target; two remain after ten attempts.

E Method-Audit Findings
The method audit rejects 108 of the 1,429 physical attempts; Prompt 3 shows the judge’s instructions. Each
rejection rationale was read by hand and assigned the one finding it names as the failure; when a rationale
20


--- Page 21 ---
DecompGym
lists several issues, the label follows the one it identifies as decisive. The labels and the decisive excerpt of
each rationale are released with the analysis code.
Unproven optimality claim (96 rejections). The solver reports its solution as “optimal” on a path where its
algorithm has not proved global optimality. Typical cases map an optimal Gurobi status of the final integer
restricted master directly to “optimal”, or stop the pricing loop at an iteration or time limit and still report
optimality. Ninety-five of these rejections concern column-generation solvers and one a Benders solver. Claude
Sonnet 5 accounts for 92; GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, and Claude Opus 5 account for the other four
(Table 7). Appendix E.1 explains the rule and why it is part of the method contract.
Inactive decomposition (8 rejections). The decomposition is written but does not operate. In six Benders
solvers, the convergence test compares an infinite initial upper bound with itself, evaluates ∞≤∞as true after
the first master solve, and terminates before any subproblem is solved. Other cases include a master whose
initial columns are never attached to its constraints, so the first solve is infeasible and pricing never runs, and
a Benders master without the recourse variable in its objective, so cuts cannot influence the search.
Solution bypass (4 rejections). A reachable fallback, such as first-fit-decreasing packing or enumeration of
every admissible shift, produces the reported solution outside the decomposition.

once; P and R denote retries under regeneration and reflection. All 26 of Claude Sonnet 5’s first-attempt claims are on
column-generation instances, where 30 of its 36 first attempts fail (Figure 8).

E.1 Unproven optimality claims
Every solver reports a status label for its solution: “optimal”, “feasible”, “infeasible”, or “error”. The label
“optimal” asserts that no better solution exists. The method contract, given identically to every agent and to the
judge, ends with the sentence “Use status feasible when returning an incumbent without a global optimality
proof; optimality of an integer restricted master alone does not prove global optimality” (highlighted in
Prompts 1 and 3). The quality criterion checks the objective value and not the status label, so a solver that
reports “feasible” can meet all three criteria: 115 of the 1,080 attempts that met all three criteria, including 70
column-generation solvers, reported “feasible” (Table 8). The reference implementations themselves report
“feasible” on 27 of the 81 instances (Appendix A). An unproven optimality claim is rejected because the
algorithm has not established it.
Table 8. Status reported by the 1,080 attempts that met all three criteria, by decomposition method. Each attempt is
counted once, including the shared first attempt.
Reported status
Benders
Column generation
All
optimal
548
417
965
feasible
45
70
115
All successful attempts
593
487
1,080
Consider cutting stock, a minimization problem. Let Ω be the set of all feasible cutting patterns, 𝐾⊆Ω the
patterns generated so far, and 𝑧★the optimal number of stock pieces. Column generation solves the linear
relaxation of the master over 𝐾and prices new patterns with its duals. Two bounds apply.
• If pricing proves that no pattern in Ω has negative reduced cost, the restricted linear value equals the full
linear relaxation value 𝑧LP, and 𝑧LP ≤𝑧★. This is a valid lower bound. If pricing stopped early at an iteration
or time limit, the restricted value does not certify a lower bound.
21


--- Page 22 ---
DecompGym
• Solving the restricted master as an integer program over 𝐾gives a feasible solution with value 𝑧IP(𝐾) ≥𝑧★.
This is an upper bound. Gurobi’s “optimal” status for this solve means only that no better integer solution
exists using the patterns in 𝐾. Solving the integer restricted master once after the linear relaxation has
converged is the heuristic known as price-and-branch [43].
Hence 𝑧LP ≤𝑧★≤𝑧IP(𝐾). Because the objective is integer, the solution is proved optimal when 𝑧IP(𝐾) = ⌈𝑧LP⌉.
Otherwise the gap is unresolved: the optimal integer solution may need a pattern that pricing never generated,
because pricing selects patterns that improve the linear relaxation and does not consider the integer program.
Branch-and-price closes such a gap by continuing to generate columns inside branch-and-bound [4, 43]. A
solver that reports the integer master’s optimal status as “optimal” for the whole problem conflates optimality
over 𝐾with optimality over Ω. The same reasoning applies to the other column-generation families, and an
analogous argument, in which the Benders master supplies the lower bound, applies to the single Benders
case. Section 5.3 applies the argument to a cutting-stock instance.
A reported optimality status is a correctness claim that users act on, for example by stopping a search
or trusting a bound, so an unproven optimality claim is an error even when the objective happens to be
optimal. Because the rule decides one model’s standing, Table 9 reports every model’s success counts with
these rejections counted as passes; Section 5.6 summarizes the changes, and the reflection counts at budgets
three and ten are unchanged.

optimality claims counted as passes when the output was otherwise feasible and within 1% of the optimal objective. A
trajectory stops at its first success, so the relaxed counts follow each saved trajectory up to its first accepted attempt. P
denotes independent regeneration and R reflection.

H Time and Token Accounting
Agent time sums the generation and reflection calls of each trajectory up to its first success or its tenth attempt,
so Table 4 averages over all 81 instances, including trajectories that exhaust the budget. A reflection after
attempt 𝑡counts toward the cost of attempt 𝑡+ 1, and attempts after a success add nothing. Figure 12 adds
the time of the method audit and of solver execution. All times are recorded stage durations. They exclude
user pauses and waits for scheduling or provider usage limits. Because stages ran in parallel, their sum differs
from the wall-clock duration of the experiment. Calls that failed without producing an attempt remain in the
raw call records and are excluded from these totals.

Recorded tokens follow each tool’s accounting. For Codex, the total is input plus output tokens, and cached
input is already part of input. For Claude Code, it is the sum of ordinary input tokens, tokens written to and
read from the prompt cache, and output tokens. Reasoning tokens are part of output and are not added again.
Counts accumulate over the agent’s turns, so they measure the total volume processed over all turns; the
providers also use different tokenizers. Table 4 and Figure 6 therefore report tokens for the eleven models
with comparable totals.
Gemini’s tool records output, thinking, cache-read, and its own total tokens, but not how cache reads
relate to input, so no comparable total can be formed. Table 13 reports the mean recorded output, thinking,
cache-read, and provider-total tokens. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains in every attempt and time comparison.

I Configuration and Reproducibility
The experiment uses Codex 0.162.1, Claude Code 2.1.296, and Google Antigravity 1.3.1. The generated solver
environment uses Python 3.12.11, Gurobi 11.0.3, and macOS 26.4.1. The attempt limit is ten per policy, each
agent call is limited to 900 seconds, and each solver run is limited to 60 seconds with one numerical solver
thread. Each generation, reflection, and judge call runs in a new Docker container limited to one CPU and 1
GB of memory, with a newly created workspace. The agent tools run without persistent state: Codex with
ephemeral sessions and user configuration and rules ignored; Claude Code without session persistence, MCP
servers, or slash commands, and with tools limited to reading and editing files; Antigravity in a new project
with its sandbox enabled. Generated solvers run outside the containers, on the host under the macOS sandbox.
The machine runs two instances at a time, with at most two simultaneous agent calls for Codex and one each
for Claude and Gemini. All generation and reflection calls use medium reasoning effort, and the method judge
requests GPT-6 Astra at high effort. Model labels identify the requested models; the Antigravity tool does not
independently report which model served a call.
The results combine two runs with the same instances, prompts, scoring code, and resource limits. The
first contains the five GPT models, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5; the second
adds Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Fable 5. The released records identify
the protocol of each run and contain all 972 complete model–instance pairs of the twelve models in Table 2.
Appendix A reports the validation of the reference implementations.
The released analysis gives, for each instance, the first successful attempt, the success counts at every
attempt budget, and the time and token totals. Every plotted count is checked against the paired outcomes,
including the nesting 𝑄≤𝑉≤𝐸and the equality of the shared first-attempt scores across policies. Each
model keeps one color, marker, and line style across figures, and panels that compare the two policies place
regeneration on the left and reflection on the right, on matched axes. An index links each figure to its source
data.
J Prompt Examples
The prompts below come from the case study in Section 5.3: Claude Sonnet 5, through Claude Code, on the
medium cutting-stock instance with seed 0. The judge prompt is the one GPT-6 Astra received for that attempt.
Codex receives identical text. The Antigravity tool receives the same task and context with its workspace rules
merged into one line, which also bars the agent from saved memory, add-on skills, helper agents, and earlier
conversations. Every prompt is verbatim except where gray text marks an elided context block. The sentence
printed in red is the status requirement discussed in Appendix E.1; the colors are added for the reader, and
the agents received plain text. Table 14 summarizes what each call receives.
J.1 Generation
Prompt 1 is the full first-attempt prompt, with the instance data abbreviated. Regeneration retries receive
the same text in a fresh call. The task description and output format are family-specific; the method contract
consists of one method-specific paragraph followed by three paragraphs shared by all nine families. Prompt 2
shows the method-specific paragraph that Benders families receive in its place.

Prompt 8
Prompt 1: Generation prompt (cutting stock, column generation)
Only edit the existing solver.py in the current working directory. All task context is supplied below.
Do not inspect other directories, use external tools or services, or search for reference implementations.
Do not execute the generated solver. The harness executes it later in its documented runtime directory.
Keep prose paragraphs and list items on one physical line; rely on editor soft wrapping.
You are an expert operations research engineer and Python programmer.
You are given a 1D cutting stock problem:
- Stock length W = 247 cm.
- Item types i=0..m-1, each with width size[i] and demand demand[i].
- Objective: minimize number of stock pieces used.
Context: a manufacturing operation cutting stock material into ordered widths.
Input file data.json contains:
- "stock_size" (or "roll_width"), "stock_unit"
- "item_types": list of { "id": int, "name": str, "size": int, "demand": int }
Examples from this instance:
- PaperProduct_0 (id=0, size=137, demand=41)
- PaperProduct_1 (id=1, size=77, demand=35)
- PaperProduct_2 (id=2, size=29, demand=60)
- PaperProduct_3 (id=3, size=57, demand=29)
- ...
Task:
Assume gurobipy and NumPy are available; the Python standard library is also allowed. Do not depend on any files other than data.json.
Write a Python program solver.py that:
1) loads data.json,
2) Implements a Column Generation to solve the cutting stock problem,
3) writes output.json with at least:
{
"status": "optimal | feasible | infeasible | error",
"method": "column_generation",
"objective_value": <#stock pieces used>,
"solution": {
"patterns": [
{
"pattern_id": <int>,
"usage": <int>,
"cuts": [
{
"item_id": <int>,
"count": <int>
},
...
]
},
...
]
}
}
Each pattern's total width must not exceed stock_size. Across all patterns (accounting for usage) every item demand must be met.
Decomposition method requirements:
28


--- Page 29 ---
DecompGym
Use a restricted master problem and pricing subproblems. Use master dual or reduced-cost information to generate columns, add useful
columns to the restricted master, and reoptimize iteratively. A final integer solve of the restricted master over the accumulated
columns is allowed. Construct the reported solution from this column-generation procedure.
Do not build and solve a separate monolithic optimization model of the full original problem, including for an initial incumbent,
initialization, a warm start, a fallback, the reported solution, or an optimality certificate. This prohibition includes a
full-original-model feasibility solve with a zero objective and applies to every reachable solution-producing path, including
conditional fallback paths, even when decomposition also runs.
Heuristic initialization, directly constructed seed columns, phase-I restricted masters with artificial variables and pricing, valid
initial bounds or cuts, and warm-starting a legitimate decomposition master are allowed. A permitted initialization must not obtain its
solution from a separate full-original-model solve. The restriction concerns that separate full model, not legitimate decomposition
masters, fixed-decision subproblems, pricing problems, or integer restricted masters.
Implement the information feedback required by the requested method. There is no minimum iteration count and no requirement that every
instance add a cut or column, or improve the initial incumbent: legitimate immediate convergence or termination is allowed. Report
mutually consistent decisions and objective values from the same incumbent. Use status feasible when returning an incumbent without a
global optimality proof; optimality of an integer restricted master alone does not prove global optimality.
The data below are provided as read-only context for this editing call.
The generated solver.py will be executed later in a separate runtime directory, where it must read ../../data.json and write
output.json in that runtime directory.
Implement a standalone solver.py using gurobipy, NumPy, and the Python standard library. Write output.json using the documented
contract. Do not import repository implementations or load reference solutions.
The harness limits the entire solver.py execution to 60 seconds and numerical solvers to 1 thread(s). Design your algorithm and
termination handling within this budget.

"demand": 41
},
{
"id": 1,
"name": "PaperProduct_1",
"size": 77,

Prompt 2: Method-specific contract paragraph for Benders families (shown for UFL)
Decomposition method requirements:
Use a master problem for the complicating decisions and recourse-cost estimates. Solve subproblems with the master decisions fixed, and
use subproblem information to generate feasibility or optimality cuts and update subsequent master solves. Classical, integer, and
logic-based Benders decomposition are allowed; LP duals are not required for integer or logic-based variants. Solving the master and
fixed-decision subproblems as LPs or MIPs is allowed. Construct the reported solution from this decomposition, retaining a feasible
incumbent when appropriate.

Prompt 3: Method-judge prompt
Only edit the existing alg_verifier.md in the current working directory. All task context is supplied below.
Do not inspect other directories, use external tools or services, or search for reference implementations.
Do not execute the generated solver. The harness executes it later in its documented runtime directory.
Keep prose paragraphs and list items on one physical line; rely on editor soft wrapping.
Inspect the supplied solver.py and determine whether it implements column generation and substantively uses that method to produce the
reported solution. Apply the following method contract, which is also supplied to the solver author:
Decomposition method requirements:
Use a restricted master problem and pricing subproblems. Use master dual or reduced-cost information to generate columns, add useful
columns to the restricted master, and reoptimize iteratively. A final integer solve of the restricted master over the accumulated
columns is allowed. Construct the reported solution from this column-generation procedure.
Do not build and solve a separate monolithic optimization model of the full original problem, including for an initial incumbent,
initialization, a warm start, a fallback, the reported solution, or an optimality certificate. This prohibition includes a
full-original-model feasibility solve with a zero objective and applies to every reachable solution-producing path, including
conditional fallback paths, even when decomposition also runs.
Heuristic initialization, directly constructed seed columns, phase-I restricted masters with artificial variables and pricing, valid
initial bounds or cuts, and warm-starting a legitimate decomposition master are allowed. A permitted initialization must not obtain its
solution from a separate full-original-model solve. The restriction concerns that separate full model, not legitimate decomposition
masters, fixed-decision subproblems, pricing problems, or integer restricted masters.
Implement the information feedback required by the requested method. There is no minimum iteration count and no requirement that every
instance add a cut or column, or improve the initial incumbent: legitimate immediate convergence or termination is allowed. Report
mutually consistent decisions and objective values from the same incumbent. Use status feasible when returning an incumbent without a
global optimality proof; optimality of an integer restricted master alone does not prove global optimality.
Trace the entry point, relevant reachable call paths, information passed back to the master, and the code that writes output.json.
Method names, comments, unused decomposition functions, or loops that do not feed subproblem information back into the master are
insufficient. For an initialization or final solve, identify which decisions are fixed, which variables or columns are optimized, and
where its result is used; an LP or MIP call by itself is not a violation.
Return FAIL if a reachable solution-producing path uses a prohibited separate full-original-model solve, even if decomposition also
runs. For conditional fallbacks, cite the triggering conditions and role from source without assuming they ran. Unused helpers or
provably unreachable branches alone are not a reason for FAIL. A genuine decomposition can converge or stop without adding a cut or
column in a particular instance, and may return its initialized feasible incumbent.
This is an algorithm-use assessment, not a full mathematical proof of every cut, bound, or pricing formulation. Execution, feasibility,
output consistency, and objective quality are checked separately. An incorrect numerical result alone is not a reason for algorithm
FAIL; determine whether the requested decomposition is substantively implemented and used. Do not require a particular cut
construction, initialization heuristic, pricing algorithm, or number of iterations.
Do not execute or modify solver.py. Do not claim to have observed runtime behavior when reviewing source only. Write alg_verifier.md
with exactly a first line VERDICT: PASS or VERDICT: FAIL, followed by NOTES: and concise code evidence supporting the verdict.

Prompt 4: Judge rationale for Claude Sonnet 5, attempt 1 (the method-audit output)
VERDICT: FAIL
NOTES:
- The source substantively implements column generation: `main()` constructs single-item seed patterns, solves a continuous restricted
master over `patterns`, passes demand-constraint duals (`c.Pi`) to a single-stock knapsack pricing problem, and appends a new pattern
when its dual value exceeds `1.0 + 1e-6`; subsequent iterations rebuild and reoptimize the master with that column.
- Initialization directly constructs columns. The final integer master fixes each accumulated pattern's item counts and optimizes only
its usage (`y_vars`). No separate full-original-model solve appears on any reachable path; time, iteration, master-status, and pricing
termination paths proceed with the accumulated patterns.
- The explicit status/proof requirement is violated: `if final.Status == GRB.OPTIMAL: status = "optimal"` treats optimality of the
integer restricted master as global optimality. This reachable branch requires no global bound comparison or other global proof,
including after early column-generation termination. Such an incumbent must be reported as `feasible` unless global optimality is
established.
- The successful `output.json` path derives pattern usages from `y_vars[p_idx].X` and the objective from their sum, but writes the
unsupported `optimal` status above. The no-incumbent and exception paths write error results. This assessment is based solely on the
supplied source; the solver was not executed.

Prompt 7: Reflection advice written by Claude Sonnet 5 after attempt 1 (the reflection advice file)
# Debug Reflection -- attempt_01
## Diagnosis
The verifier failed the attempt on a single concrete defect: the final status-reporting logic conflates "integer restricted master
solved to optimality" with "global optimality." The line `if final.Status == GRB.OPTIMAL: status = "optimal"` reports `optimal`
whenever the final integer solve over the accumulated columns terminates optimally, but this only proves optimality of the restricted
master (a subset of all possible cutting patterns), not of the original cutting-stock problem. Since the LP relaxation's column
generation loop stops as soon as no column has reduced cost > 1 (i.e., LP-optimal for the restricted set), and the integer master is
then solved separately, there is no global lower bound (e.g., ceil(LP relaxation objective) compared against the integer incumbent, or
proof that no further columns could improve the integer solution) ever computed or checked. So the reported "optimal" status is
unsupported -- everything else in the algorithm (seed patterns, dual-based knapsack pricing, iterative column addition, final integer
solve) was judged structurally sound and compliant with the decomposition requirements.
## Root cause
Status assignment used local (restricted master) optimality as a proxy for global optimality without any certificate.
## Concrete changes for next attempt
1. Always report `status = "feasible"` for the incumbent produced by the final integer restricted-master solve, unless a genuine
global optimality certificate is constructed (e.g., comparing the final integer objective to a valid lower bound such as ceil(final LP
relaxation bound) AND confirming the pricing loop terminated because no improving column exists at the LP optimum, not merely because
of a time/iteration cutoff).
2. Simplest compliant fix: unconditionally set `status = "feasible"` when returning any incumbent from the integer restricted master,
since optimality of that integer program does not prove global optimality of the original cutting-stock problem (as stated explicitly
in the task requirements). Only use `"optimal"` if the column-generation loop provably converged (no improving column exists, i.e.,
pricing objective <= 1 + tol) AND the final integer master's objective equals the LP relaxation's rounded-up bound -- otherwise default
to `"feasible"`.
3. Keep all other logic (seed patterns, duals from master, knapsack pricing subproblem, final integer solve over accumulated columns)
unchanged -- it already satisfies the decomposition requirements and avoids any monolithic full-model solve.
4. Double check: if `sub.Status == GRB.TIME_LIMIT` is used to break the loop (not a proven no-improving-column condition), that path
must also report `"feasible"`, not `"optimal"`.
